The patient presents with a subacute, progressive neurological syndrome characterized by:

- Profound immunosuppression (CD4 <100/μL)

This is a classic presentation of HIV-associated Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML). The patient’s profound immunosuppression (CD4 56/μL, high VL) places him at highest risk for JC virus reactivation. Critically, the brain MRI shows *disseminated, nonenhancing, asymmetric white matter lesions without mass effect or edema* — the hallmark neuroimaging signature of PML. Enhancement would suggest alternative diagnoses (e.g., lymphoma, toxoplasmosis, or IRIS), while mass effect/edema would raise concern for tumor or abscess. The absence of systemic infection signs, meningeal symptoms, or CSF pleocytosis further disfavors infectious mimics. Although CSF JC virus PCR is the diagnostic gold standard, the clinical-radiologic constellation in this severely immunocompromised host is *highly specific* for PML — meeting established diagnostic criteria (probable PML per EFNS/PML Consortium guidelines when MRI + clinical features align in immunosuppressed patients, even pre-PCR). - **CNS toxoplasmosis**: Typically enhances, involves basal ganglia/cortex, and presents with headache/fever — absent here.  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML)

[THOUGHT]  
This is a classic presentation of HIV-associated Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML). The patient’s profound immunosuppression (CD4 56/μL, high VL) places him at highest risk for JC virus reactivation. The subacute–chronic cognitive-behavioral decline over 6 months — including memory loss, disorientation, paranoia, and agitation — reflects progressive subcortical dementia, consistent with frontal-subcortical circuit disruption by white matter demyelination. The acute/subacute right leg weakness and gait instability (~1 week) represent evolving motor tract involvement (e.g., corticospinal tract in parietal or corona radiata white matter). Critically, the brain MRI shows *disseminated, nonenhancing, asymmetric white matter lesions without mass effect or edema* — the hallmark neuroimaging signature of PML. Enhancement would suggest alternative diagnoses (e.g., lymphoma, toxoplasmosis, or IRIS), while mass effect/edema would raise concern for tumor or abscess. The absence of systemic infection signs, meningeal symptoms, or CSF pleocytosis further disfavors infectious mimics. Although CSF JC virus PCR is the diagnostic gold standard, the clinical-radiologic constellation in this severely immunocompromised host is *highly specific* for PML — meeting established diagnostic criteria (probable PML per EFNS/PML Consortium guidelines when MRI + clinical features align in immunosuppressed patients, even pre-PCR). ART initiation is not merely supportive but disease-modifying and urgent.
